title: Savaiye close
hook: the ten verses sharpen one point: love, not display

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line at the heart of the savaiye, and yours: those who loved, found. Did you love someone out loud? Today we close the ten verses. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

Here's a strange thing about the man who wrote the ten savaiye. Guru Gobind Singh is the Guru who gave the Khalsa its outward form. The five articles that Sikhs who take amrit keep on their bodies every day: uncut hair, a comb, a steel bracelet, cotton undershorts, the kirpan. He shaped how a whole community looks, to this day. And the same Guru wrote ten verses saying outward forms, without love, aren't worth a single seed. Is that a contradiction? Sikhs have an answer, and it's the best way to close these ten verses. Today: Savaiye close.
screen: `THE GURU WHO GAVE THE KHALSA ITS FORM.` → `WROTE THAT FORM WITHOUT LOVE IS NOTHING.` → `A CONTRADICTION?`

segments.voice: Start by laying the ten verses side by side. They make the same move every time. Set up something impressive, then weigh it. Tav prasad, by your grace, over the door. The ascetics of every order, weighed: not one ratti without love. The elephants in gold: their kings left barefoot. The conquerors with their drums: the beat faded. The crane with its eyes shut: still, and hunting. Every outward ritual, compassion and charity included: the secret missed. And then the line the set leans on: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. Ten verses, one point, sharpened until it cuts. Love, not display. Now the question from the hook. Sikhs don't hear the savaiye as saying the outward form doesn't matter. The same verses are recited while the amrit is prepared, at the very ceremony where people take on the five articles. So the form and the warning are given in the same breath, on purpose. The way many Sikhs put it, the form is meant to carry the love, the way a cup carries water. A beautiful cup that's empty is still empty. But nobody throws away the cup because of that. They fill it. The danger the savaiye name is the cup admired for itself: the turban worn for show, the bani rushed to be done, the kirpan as a costume. And the savaiye don't let anyone off. Not kings, not yogis, not pilgrims, and not the Khalsa. That's the strength of these ten verses. Their writer aimed them at his own people first.
screen: `TEN VERSES, ONE MOVE: WEIGH IT.` · `LOVE, NOT DISPLAY.` · `SAID AS THE AMRIT IS PREPARED.` · `THE FORM IS A CUP FOR THE LOVE.` · then, large: `LOVE, NOT DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read your favorite one again. Settle and breathe. Think back over this week's verses: the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane, the rituals, the line about love. Which one stayed with you? If you have the text or a recording, go to it and read or listen to that one savaiya again, slowly. If you don't, just replay its picture in your mind. Then ask what it was about that one that caught you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you've finished. The bell holds the time.
Savaiye close. Ten verses that weigh the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane and every ritual, and find only love was ever heavy enough.
Your line: love, not display. Today, look at one thing you wear or keep that means something to you, and ask whether it's carrying love or just being admired. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib; they are also read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation, where initiates take on the five articles of faith.

fork.setup: a friend says: if the savaiye say outward forms are worthless, why does the same Guru ask the Khalsa to keep five articles? how would many Sikhs answer?
options: the savaiye were written by someone else.
the form is a cup for the love; the warning is against an empty cup.
the five articles are only for show.
fork.reveal: the savaiye are recited as the amrit is prepared, form and warning given together. many Sikhs say the form carries the love, and the danger is the cup admired for itself.

original.note: Gurmukhi: savaiye, the plural of savaiya, the four-line verse form of these ten.

trapdoor: what you thought: ten poems saying religion is all show.
what it means: ten verses with one point, love, not display, said at the very ceremony where the Khalsa takes on its form.
what a scholar hears: the ten form a set inside the Akal Ustat, each built on the same weighing, and their use in the amrit ceremony binds the outward form and the inward warning together.
